reader.title: Threatened lynching of Loula Tyler
bases: A1 reports that Loula Tyler, accused of assaulting a child, was 'with difficulty' saved from lynching by people infuriated at the child's injuries, a threatened lynching in which no one was killed.
A1 says Tyler was saved from lynching and was jailed alive to await the grand jury, so no one was killed; the threat arose from the accusation that she had choked a child.
Only the Memphis Public Ledger (A1) reported the episode; no second account or follow-up was found.

summary.text: The threatened lynching of Loula Tyler took place near White's Station, east of Memphis, on 22 December 1881, when a Black girl of about seventeen accused of choking a schoolgirl was 'with difficulty' saved from lynching.
She was jailed in Memphis to await the grand jury; the episode is known from a single Memphis Public Ledger report.
Sallie Moore, nine or ten years old and the daughter of the widow Pattie G. Moore, was walking alone to school that morning and crossing the railway near her home.

According to the child's account as printed in the Public Ledger, Tyler grabbed her by the hair, dragged her into a ditch and choked her until Mary Dennis, 'a colored woman', heard her and drove Tyler away.
The paper reported that the marks on the child made 'all who saw her' infuriated and that Tyler was barely saved from lynching; it did not say who threatened her, how many, or who protected her.
Major Dick Mason, whose office the paper did not give, arrested Tyler and held her overnight at his residence a mile or two from the station.
The next morning she was taken to the Memphis jail to await the grand jury.
Tyler told her captors that she had acted to protect the girl from 'a big haired man' lying in wait for the child.
Because no one else was reported near the spot, the Public Ledger said the theory was that she was 'either crazy or feigning lunacy'.
No report of grand jury action, a trial or any later disposition of the case was found.
The Public Ledger ran the story on its front page on 23 December under the headline 'A BAD DARKY / Chokes a Little Girl Half to Death'.
It called Tyler a 'violent tempered female crank', a 'yellow girl', a 'wench' and a 'bad tempered piece', and the child a 'helpless and innocent victim'.
It presented the child's version as fact and gave the threatened lynching a single sentence, without comment.
No other paper's account, white or Black, appears in the coverage.

accounts.label: Child's account as narrated by the Public Ledger
accounts.gist: Sallie Moore said Tyler grabbed her by the hair, dragged her into a ditch and choked her until Mary Dennis drove Tyler off.

accounts.label: Loula Tyler's explanation
accounts.gist: Tyler said she acted to protect the girl from 'a big haired man' lying in wait for the child; the paper dismissed this because no one else was reported near the spot.

framing.detail: The Public Ledger headlined the story 'A BAD DARKY', called Tyler a 'wench' and 'bad tempered piece' from a family 'of the same caliber', presented the child's account as fact, and mentioned the near-lynching in one sentence without comment on those who threatened it.

record_check.dossier: Accused of half choking Sallie Moore, 'nine or ten years' old; the paper does not state the child's race.
Black by the paper's terms ('A BAD DARKY', 'yellow girl'), not stated in words.
Not stated; about nine miles east of Memphis.
Not stated; implied Tennessee (near Memphis, Memphis paper).
Arrested by Major Dick Mason, held at his residence overnight, then jailed in Memphis to await the grand jury; the paper does not say whether the threat came before or after her arrest.
'All who saw' the injured child; unnamed and of unstated number and race.

record_check.record: Enraged onlookers nearly lynched her, and she was saved with difficulty before being arrested and jailed.
record_check.dossier: The paper says only that 'it was with difficulty that Loula Tyler was saved from lynching'; it does not describe a mob action, who saved her, or the order of the threat and the arrest.

info: The alleged assault took place on the morning of 22 December 1881 ('yesterday morning' in a 23 December paper); the threat of lynching followed the same day.
A few hundred yards from White's Station, about nine miles east of Memphis, where the child crossed the railway on her way to school.
Loula Tyler, about seventeen years old, reared near White's Station; the paper calls her a 'yellow girl' and 'wench' under the headline 'A BAD DARKY'.
Accused of seizing Sallie Moore, nine or ten years old, by the hair, dragging her into a ditch and half choking her.
Those who saw the marks on the child, 'all who saw her became infuriated'; no names, race or number given.
Tyler was in jail in Memphis as of 23 December 1881; no later report was found.

sources.note: Only report: 'A BAD DARKY'; Loula Tyler accused of choking Sallie Moore near White's Station; 'with difficulty' saved from lynching; arrested by Major Dick Mason and jailed in Memphis to await the grand jury.
quotes: The marks of the assault were so plainly visible on the child that all who saw her became infuriated, and it was with difficulty that Loula Tyler was saved from lynching.
The only explanation given by the wench for her conduct was that she did it to protect the girl from a big haired man who was lying in wait for the child.
A violent tempered female crank rests in jail on a very serious charge.
